subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 26-year-old at 21 weeks of gestation has newly diagnosed syphilis requiring treatment. She previously had immediate urticaria, wheezing, and hypotension after penicillin, and specialist assessment confirms an IgE-mediated allergy. She has no history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome or another severe delayed reaction. Maternal vital signs are currently normal. Which plan best addresses both the infection and the confirmed allergy?

options.text: Defer maternal treatment until after delivery to avoid all fetal drug exposure
options.explanation: Untreated maternal infection can harm the fetus during pregnancy, so waiting until after delivery sacrifices the opportunity for timely fetal protection.

options.text: Arrange monitored desensitization followed by the stage-appropriate penicillin regimen
options.explanation: Penicillin is the proven therapy for fetal protection in pregnancy; confirmed immediate allergy requires a supervised desensitization pathway rather than an unproven substitute.

options.text: Give doxycycline throughout pregnancy as an equivalent proven fetal-protective alternative
options.explanation: Doxycycline is not the recommended equivalent treatment for syphilis in pregnancy and does not replace the established penicillin-based prevention of fetal infection.

options.text: Give penicillin immediately without supervision because allergy history never matters
options.explanation: Her confirmed immediate allergy creates a genuine risk; effective treatment must include an appropriate monitored desensitization strategy rather than disregarding the reaction.

explanation: Parenteral penicillin G is the only therapy with documented efficacy for treating fetal infection and preventing congenital syphilis. A pregnant patient with confirmed immediate allergy therefore needs specialist-directed desensitization and the penicillin regimen appropriate to her disease stage. The stem excludes severe delayed hypersensitivity because that requires a different allergy assessment and should not be treated as routine IgE desensitization. Maternal stability does not justify delaying infection treatment until delivery. The clinical team must plan monitoring and emergency readiness rather than presenting desensitization as a casual unsupervised dose.
objective: Preserve effective maternal-fetal syphilis treatment while managing confirmed immediate penicillin allergy.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 33-year-old with known endometriosis has an adnexal cyst evaluated by ultrasonography. The report describes features compatible with an endometrioma and no ascites or suspicious solid vascular nodule. A CA-125 ordered elsewhere is mildly elevated. She has no weight loss or progressive abdominal distention and believes the blood result proves ovarian cancer. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.explanation: Endometriosis can elevate CA-125, so a modest result cannot independently establish malignancy or replace a structured assessment of the adnexal lesion.

stem: A 31-year-old breastfeeding her 4-month-old notices a firm focal breast lump that remains after feeds and pumping. It has persisted for 3 weeks. subject: Medicine
stem: A 32-year-old has 18 months of infertility. Ovulation has been reasonably established, and her partner's semen evaluation is reassuring. She had treated chlamydial PID several years ago but now has no pelvic pain or signs of infection. Pregnancy is excluded, and she has no relevant contrast allergy. options.text: A routine cervical cytology sample

subject: Medicine
stem: A 29-year-old reports irritability, bloating, and breast discomfort that she believes occur before each period. She is unsure whether symptoms fully disappear afterward. There is no suicidal ideation, mania, or functional emergency, and an initial assessment finds no clear medical cause. She requests a definitive premenstrual diagnosis based on her memory of the last year. Which next diagnostic step is most informative?

subject: Medicine
stem: A 43-year-old receiving immunosuppressive therapy was told that a vulvar growth was a wart. Despite an appropriate treatment trial, it enlarges and develops spontaneous bleeding. Examination shows an indurated lesion with a small ulcer and fixation to underlying tissue, unlike the surrounding soft papules. She is afebrile and stable. Which next step best clarifies the concerning lesion?

options.text: Obtain a biopsy of the atypical lesion
options.explanation: Induration, ulceration, bleeding, fixation, and nonresponse are reasons to obtain tissue rather than presume a benign wart, particularly with immunosuppression.

options.text: Continue indefinite destructive wart treatment without sampling
options.explanation: Repeated destruction can delay identifying high-grade disease or carcinoma when the morphology and treatment course already make the initial visual label uncertain.

options.text: Order an HPV antibody test as a substitute for tissue diagnosis
options.explanation: An antibody result does not characterize the invasive potential or histology of this focal atypical lesion and cannot replace a biopsy.

options.text: Declare malignancy excluded because other nearby lesions look like warts
options.explanation: Benign-appearing surrounding papules do not establish the nature of a separate indurated ulcerated lesion, and mixed pathology can occur at adjacent sites.

explanation: Most anogenital warts are diagnosed clinically, but atypical lesions require a different approach. CDC identifies pigmentation, induration, fixation, bleeding, and ulceration as findings that support biopsy, and immunocompromise or treatment failure adds concern. Tissue assessment distinguishes a wart from high-grade squamous disease or invasive cancer. This diagnostic step does not mean that every wart is malignant or that appearance alone proves cancer. The clinical priority is resolving uncertainty before further destructive treatment obscures a lesion whose behavior is no longer typical.
objective: Recognize when an apparent anogenital wart requires tissue diagnosis.
keyPoints: Atypical morphology can override an earlier visual wart diagnosis.
Nonresponse and immunosuppression strengthen the need for reassessment.

subject: Pathology
stem: A 47-year-old notices a firm breast lump several weeks after a seat-belt injury. Diagnostic imaging shows an oil-containing lesion at the bruised site. Because an adjacent finding was initially uncertain, core sampling is performed. It shows disrupted adipocytes, foamy macrophages, and fibrosis without malignant cells, and the radiologist judges the tissue and imaging concordant. Which diagnosis best explains the lesion?

options.text: Invasive ductal carcinoma proven by any firm post-traumatic lump
options.explanation: Firmness alone does not establish carcinoma, and the concordant imaging and biopsy specifically show adipocyte injury without malignant epithelial invasion.

options.text: Acute bacterial breast abscess
options.explanation: An abscess would be supported by purulent fluid and infection findings rather than an oil-containing lesion with damaged fat cells and no described infection.

options.text: A normal lactational milk-retention cyst
options.explanation: The patient is not lactating, and the sampled material reflects injured adipose tissue rather than retained breast milk within a duct-associated cyst.

options.text: Fat necrosis of the breast
options.explanation: Traumatic adipocyte injury can form an oil-containing mass with macrophage reaction and fibrosis, producing a benign lesion that may mimic malignancy clinically.

explanation: Breast fat necrosis is a benign response to adipose injury that may follow trauma, surgery, or radiation. It can produce a firm lump, skin changes, or imaging findings that mimic cancer, so a history of trauma alone must not be used to dismiss a suspicious mass. Here the oil-containing appearance and biopsy findings are concordant, supporting fat necrosis. The histology differs from an invasive epithelial malignancy or infection. Further follow-up should follow the actual imaging-pathology assessment; discordance would require additional evaluation rather than reassurance based only on the benign label.
objective: Recognize concordant breast fat-necrosis findings without using trauma history alone to exclude cancer.
keyPoints: Fat necrosis can mimic a malignant breast mass.
Imaging-pathology concordance matters when accepting a benign biopsy.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 61-year-old is evaluated for intermittent thick green-brown nipple discharge. There is mild subareolar discomfort without fever or an enlarging mass. Diagnostic mammography and ultrasound show dilated subareolar ducts containing debris without a suspicious focal lesion. Breast assessment finds the imaging and examination concordant with a benign ductal process. Which diagnosis best fits the observed structural abnormality?

options.text: Acute puerperal mastitis
options.explanation: She is not postpartum or lactating and has no febrile inflammatory presentation to support an acute puerperal breast infection as the best explanation.

options.text: A proven invasive cancer solely because the discharge is brown
options.explanation: Discharge color alone cannot establish malignancy, and the specified diagnostic assessment supports a benign ductal process rather than a biopsy-proven invasive tumor.

options.text: Mammary duct ectasia
options.explanation: Dilated subareolar ducts with thick retained secretions fit duct ectasia, a benign process that can cause colored discharge and local discomfort around menopause.

options.text: Prolactinoma established by any colored nipple discharge
options.explanation: Prolactin-related galactorrhea is typically milky and does not by itself explain the documented debris-containing dilated ducts or establish a pituitary tumor.

explanation: Mammary duct ectasia involves widening of ducts, often beneath the nipple, with retained secretions and surrounding inflammatory change. It can cause thick colored discharge or discomfort in a patient around or after menopause. The case supplies a diagnostic assessment and concordant benign findings because discharge characteristics alone do not safely exclude malignancy. A new spontaneous unilateral bloody discharge, focal suspicious lesion, or discordant clinical course would require further workup. The distinction from galactorrhea is the demonstrated structural duct change rather than a conclusion drawn simply from the patient's age.
objective: Recognize mammary duct ectasia after concordant evaluation of thick colored nipple discharge.
keyPoints: Duct ectasia can produce thick colored secretions.
A benign explanation requires concordance with the actual breast assessment.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 30-year-old at 30 weeks of gestation has confirmed iron-deficiency anemia. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL and ferritin is very low. Two appropriate oral formulations and a supervised schedule adjustment have caused vomiting and severe constipation, preventing sustained use. There is no active bleeding, hemodynamic instability, or cardiac symptom. Dietary review and evaluation for other anemia causes are complete. Which next treatment discussion is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop replacement permanently because a better diet always corrects anemia before delivery
options.explanation: Dietary optimization is useful but cannot be assumed to replete a significant deficit promptly when anemia persists and effective replacement has not been tolerated.

options.text: Discuss an appropriate intravenous iron preparation with her obstetric team
options.explanation: Persistent documented intolerance can justify intravenous replacement later in pregnancy, using an individualized formulation and monitored administration rather than repeatedly prescribing an unusable oral plan.

options.text: Continue issuing the identical oral prescription without discussing why she cannot take it
options.explanation: Repetition does not correct the documented tolerance barrier and leaves established iron deficiency inadequately treated despite several attempted oral strategies.

options.text: Give emergency red-cell transfusion solely because any pregnancy anemia requires it
options.explanation: The stem does not describe hemorrhage, instability, severe cardiopulmonary symptoms, or another urgent transfusion indication; iron replacement and transfusion are not interchangeable decisions.

explanation: Confirmed iron deficiency should be treated, but a prescription only works if the patient can receive it. After a genuine oral trial fails because of persistent intolerance, intravenous iron may be considered in the second or third trimester with attention to preparation-specific safety and administration requirements. This is different from reflexive transfusion in a stable patient without active bleeding or severe symptoms. The clinician should verify the diagnosis, prior attempts, timing, and follow-up response. The question does not specify an unverified dose or suggest that every oral adverse effect requires infusion.
objective: Address a documented oral iron tolerance barrier without confusing replacement with emergency transfusion.
keyPoints: Assess actual tolerance before repeatedly prescribing the same oral plan.
Intravenous replacement is distinct from red-cell transfusion.

subject: Physiology
stem: A 28-year-old at 27 weeks of gestation has mildly low total serum calcium on a chemistry panel. Albumin is also lower than her prepregnancy value, while directly measured ionized calcium is normal. She has no paresthesias, tetany, renal disease, or evidence of malabsorption. Her dietary calcium intake is adequate on review. Which mechanism best explains the apparently discordant calcium results?

options.text: Reduced albumin-bound calcium lowers the total measurement while the ionized fraction remains normal
options.explanation: Total calcium includes protein-bound calcium, so lower albumin can reduce that concentration without establishing a deficit of physiologically active ionized calcium.

options.text: Normal ionized calcium proves severe symptomatic calcium depletion
options.explanation: The directly measured active fraction and absence of symptoms do not support severe active hypocalcemia merely because the total measurement is mildly reduced.

options.text: Albumin carries no calcium, so its concentration cannot influence the total result
options.explanation: A substantial fraction of circulating calcium is protein-bound, making albumin relevant when interpreting total calcium concentrations in a changing physiologic state.

options.text: The placenta has removed all circulating calcium from the maternal bloodstream
options.explanation: Complete removal is incompatible with normal ionized calcium and clinical stability; the measured discrepancy is better explained by binding rather than catastrophic transfer.

explanation: Total serum calcium includes ionized, protein-bound, and complexed fractions. Albumin changes can alter the total concentration while ionized calcium remains normal. The stem provides a direct ionized measurement, avoiding the uncertainty of relying solely on an albumin correction formula. A mildly low total value in this setting does not prove inadequate dietary intake or require an automatic diagnosis of severe hypocalcemia. Clinical symptoms, renal function, vitamin D and magnesium context, and the active fraction guide further evaluation when indicated. Pregnancy does not eliminate the need to interpret the laboratory method correctly.
objective: Distinguish an albumin-related total calcium change from true ionized hypocalcemia during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Total calcium is influenced by protein binding.
Use the directly measured active fraction and clinical context when results diverge.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 25-year-old at 16 weeks of gestation is hospitalized after prolonged hyperemesis with major weight loss and minimal intake. Following rehydration, nutrition is advanced rapidly. Two days later she develops profound weakness and edema. Serum phosphate falls sharply from its pretreatment value, and potassium and magnesium also decline. There is no ongoing diarrhea, new sepsis, or renal replacement therapy. Which complication best explains the new deterioration?

options.text: An isolated mechanical bowel obstruction
options.explanation: A bowel obstruction does not best explain the coordinated electrolyte fall specifically after nutritional restoration without a new obstructive examination or imaging finding.

options.text: Normal fetal skeletal growth requiring no maternal assessment
options.explanation: Although pregnancy changes nutrient requirements, abrupt severe phosphate depletion with weakness after feeding is not a benign adaptation to be dismissed without treatment.

options.text: A medication allergy established solely by the phosphate result
options.explanation: There is no described allergic reaction, and an electrolyte-shift syndrome linked to nutritional advancement better explains the temporal and biochemical pattern.

options.text: Refeeding syndrome
options.explanation: Rapid nutrition after depletion can trigger insulin-related intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, producing weakness and fluid complications during the early refeeding interval.

explanation: Severe nutritional depletion creates vulnerability when carbohydrate and calories are restored too rapidly. Insulin-driven intracellular uptake can lower circulating phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, while fluid shifts can contribute to edema and cardiopulmonary complications. The onset shortly after feeding and the coordinated laboratory pattern support refeeding syndrome. Management requires urgent assessment, appropriate correction and monitoring, thiamine provision, and adjustment of nutrition delivery rather than abandoning nutrition indefinitely. The diagnosis should not depend on one exact universal threshold; the magnitude of change, organ effects, and clinical context matter.
objective: Recognize refeeding syndrome during nutritional rehabilitation after prolonged pregnancy vomiting.
keyPoints: The highest-risk interval can begin after feeding is restarted.
Phosphate, potassium, magnesium, thiamine, and fluid balance require coordinated attention.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 27-year-old with phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency stopped her metabolic diet years ago and now wants to conceive. Her blood phenylalanine is markedly above the metabolic clinic's target. Her partner's testing makes an affected child unlikely, so she believes no dietary preparation is needed. She is not pregnant and can delay conception. Which plan best reduces the preventable fetal risk?

options.text: Avoid all dietary protein without a metabolic nutrition plan
options.explanation: Unsupervised elimination of all protein can cause nutritional inadequacy and catabolism; appropriate treatment requires a balanced specialist-designed phenylalanine-restricted regimen.

options.text: Start dietary control only after delivery because the placenta blocks phenylalanine
options.explanation: The placenta does not provide the asserted protection; elevated maternal phenylalanine during pregnancy can cause fetal developmental harm before delivery.

options.text: Reestablish specialist-directed phenylalanine control before conception and maintain it throughout pregnancy
options.explanation: High maternal phenylalanine can harm a fetus regardless of whether it inherits PAH deficiency, making preconception metabolic and nutritional control essential.

options.text: Wait for fetal genetic testing before adjusting her diet
options.explanation: The fetus can be exposed during early development before genetic results are available, and maternal biochemical toxicity is not limited to genetically affected fetuses.

explanation: Maternal PAH deficiency creates a fetal exposure risk when phenylalanine remains elevated, even if the fetus does not have the inherited disorder. Effective prevention therefore begins before conception and continues through pregnancy with metabolic monitoring and an appropriate nutritional plan. ACOG emphasizes achieving control before pregnancy rather than waiting until fetal testing resolves inheritance. Treatment is not indiscriminate starvation or elimination of every protein source; specialist medical foods and nutrient adequacy are important. The case intentionally avoids numerical targets so that exact current ranges and individualized therapy can be confirmed by the metabolic team.
objective: Prioritize maternal phenylalanine control before conception independently of fetal inheritance probability.
keyPoints: Maternal biochemical exposure and fetal genotype are different risk questions.
Use a specialist nutrition plan that avoids both excess phenylalanine and nutritional depletion.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 31-year-old at 29 weeks of gestation has newly diagnosed gestational diabetes. Before meeting a dietitian, she removes almost every carbohydrate source from her meals. Her glucose readings decline, but she loses weight, feels weak, and has urinary ketones. She has no vomiting, acidosis, or infection. She asks whether the lower glucose numbers mean the diet should be continued unchanged. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Use prolonged fasting as the preferred way to avoid every postprandial glucose rise
options.explanation: Prolonged fasting can worsen nutritional depletion and ketosis; avoiding meals is not an appropriate substitute for an adequate individualized gestational diabetes plan.

options.text: Arrange individualized medical nutrition therapy with adequate carbohydrate and energy intake, glucose monitoring, and medication if needed
options.explanation: Treatment should support pregnancy nutrition while controlling glucose; severe restriction with weight loss and ketosis signals a need to revise the plan rather than celebrate the readings.

options.text: Continue near-total carbohydrate avoidance because glucose is the only relevant outcome
options.explanation: A lower glucose value does not prove nutritional adequacy, and the associated weakness, weight loss, and ketones require assessment of the overall pregnancy diet.

options.text: Stop glucose monitoring because nutritional treatment cannot change glucose patterns
options.explanation: Meal composition affects glucose, so monitoring remains useful when adjusting nutrition and determining whether pharmacologic treatment is needed.

explanation: Gestational diabetes care includes appropriate nutrition, activity when suitable, glucose monitoring, and medication when needed. It should not be reduced to achieving low readings at the cost of inadequate energy or carbohydrate intake. The weight loss, weakness, and ketones suggest that the self-imposed plan needs reassessment. A dietitian familiar with pregnancy can distribute suitable carbohydrate sources and help maintain nutrient adequacy. If glycemic targets remain unmet on an adequate plan, pharmacotherapy is considered rather than escalating starvation. The absence of acidosis distinguishes this counseling case from an acute ketoacidosis emergency.
objective: Protect nutritional adequacy while treating gestational diabetes instead of relying on extreme carbohydrate restriction.
keyPoints: Glucose targets do not replace pregnancy nutrition goals.
Add appropriate therapy rather than achieving control through starvation.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 24-year-old at 9 weeks of gestation has daily nausea and occasional vomiting despite small frequent meals and avoiding triggers. She keeps down fluids, has stable weight and vital signs, and has no abdominal pain, fever, hematemesis, or electrolyte abnormality. The symptoms interfere with work, and she would like medication. She takes no sedative and has no relevant drug allergy. Which initial option is most appropriate?

options.text: Pyridoxine, adding doxylamine if needed after counseling
options.explanation: Vitamin B6 with or without doxylamine is a recommended initial medication approach for uncomplicated pregnancy nausea after practical dietary measures do not provide enough relief.

options.text: Immediate parenteral nutrition without an oral medication trial
options.explanation: Her preserved intake, stable weight, and normal assessment do not justify invasive nutritional support before trying an appropriate outpatient antiemetic strategy.

options.text: Induce delivery because pregnancy nausea never responds to medication
options.explanation: Delivery is neither appropriate at this gestation nor a treatment for uncomplicated early pregnancy nausea when effective supportive and medication options are available.

options.text: Dismiss symptoms because absence of dehydration means treatment is unnecessary
options.explanation: Quality-of-life impairment matters even without severe dehydration, and stable outpatient status allows treatment rather than requiring the patient to wait for deterioration.

explanation: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy can warrant treatment before severe dehydration or weight loss develops. ACOG supports vitamin B6 as an initial medication and adding doxylamine when needed. Counseling should address the selected formulation, appropriate dosing, potential sedation, and when to seek reassessment. Stable intake and absence of red flags favor an outpatient approach here. Severe or atypical symptoms would require evaluation for dehydration and other causes. Although pyridoxine is a vitamin, this item tests an antiemetic treatment decision and is not counted as a substantive nutritional-deficiency question.
objective: Select an appropriate initial outpatient medication for persistent uncomplicated nausea of pregnancy.
keyPoints: Treat meaningful symptoms before dehydration becomes severe.
Doxylamine can cause sedation and requires practical counseling.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 27-year-old at 17 weeks of a singleton pregnancy asks to follow her friend's pregnancy eating plan. Her prepregnancy BMI was 17 kg/m2, and she has gained little weight despite resolution of early nausea. Her friend began pregnancy with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 and was given a different weight-gain goal. She is stable with no edema or chronic illness. Which counseling approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use an identical weight-gain target for all singleton pregnancies regardless of starting BMI
options.explanation: Recommended goals vary with prepregnancy BMI, so a universal target ignores a clinically relevant difference between the two patients.

options.text: Advise intentional weight loss because all pregnancy weight gain is harmful
options.explanation: This underweight patient has not shown an excessive trajectory; intentional restriction could worsen inadequate intake rather than support a healthy pregnancy.

options.text: Assume low gain proves placental failure and schedule immediate delivery
options.explanation: Weight trajectory prompts assessment but does not by itself establish placental failure or justify delivery in an otherwise stable 17-week pregnancy.

options.text: Assess her intake and weight trajectory and set a goal appropriate to her prepregnancy BMI
options.explanation: Starting BMI and the current course guide nutritional goals; copying a higher-BMI patient's plan could inadequately address this patient's pregnancy energy needs.

explanation: Pregnancy weight-gain counseling is individualized using prepregnancy BMI, the course of gain, intake, and maternal-fetal assessment. An underweight patient and a patient with obesity should not automatically receive the same target or calorie plan. This patient needs assessment of current intake and barriers, with a goal appropriate to her starting status and follow-up over time. Weight alone is not a definitive diagnosis of fetal growth restriction or placental disease. A numerical target is intentionally not required here; the tested decision is selecting the proper basis for counseling rather than applying a universal rule.
objective: Use prepregnancy BMI and longitudinal gain to individualize maternal nutrition counseling.
keyPoints: Different starting BMI categories can require different gain goals.
A weight trend prompts assessment rather than proving a specific fetal diagnosis.

subject: Physiology
stem: A 32-year-old pregnant patient needs an individualized calcium supplement because dietary intake remains inadequate. She has reduced gastric acidity after prior gastric surgery and takes a proton-pump inhibitor for a documented indication. Her nutrition team selects calcium citrate rather than an equal labeled amount of calcium carbonate taken fasting. Kidney function is normal. Which property best explains the choice?

options.text: Calcium carbonate is absorbed only through the skin
options.explanation: Both formulations are oral calcium sources, and the relevant difference concerns gastrointestinal solubility and absorption rather than an unrelated transdermal pathway.

options.text: A proton-pump inhibitor makes every calcium preparation completely unabsorbable
options.explanation: Reduced acidity can affect formulations differently; it does not establish zero uptake of every preparation or make individualized supplementation inherently futile.

options.text: Calcium citrate absorption is less dependent on gastric acid than calcium carbonate absorption
options.explanation: Lower acid availability can impair carbonate dissolution, particularly fasting, while citrate is less acid-dependent and therefore better fits the stated absorption context.

options.text: Calcium citrate contains no calcium and works only by increasing vitamin D production
options.explanation: Citrate preparations supply elemental calcium; their rationale is not an absence of calcium or direct stimulation of renal vitamin D production.

explanation: The form of a mineral supplement can affect absorption. Calcium carbonate is more dependent on gastric acidity and is generally better taken with food, whereas citrate is less dependent on stomach acid. That distinction is relevant after selected gastric procedures or during acid suppression. The amount of elemental calcium on the label still matters, along with dietary intake, divided administration when appropriate, other nutrients, and pregnancy-specific needs. Choosing citrate does not by itself guarantee adequacy after every gastric procedure; broader micronutrient monitoring may remain necessary in a patient with prior surgery.
objective: Relate reduced gastric acidity to calcium supplement formulation choice during pregnancy.
keyPoints: Calcium salt chemistry can affect uptake.
A more suitable formulation does not remove the need for nutritional follow-up.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 23-year-old at 24 weeks of gestation has inadequate weight gain. She understands the dietitian's meal plan but often skips meals so her younger children can eat. There is no persistent vomiting, swallowing difficulty, or restrictive weight-loss goal. Vital signs are stable, and fetal assessment is currently reassuring. She worries that admitting the food shortage will make the clinic judge her. Which next step best addresses the identified barrier?

options.text: Stop prenatal follow-up because social needs cannot influence medical outcomes
options.explanation: Food access affects maternal nutrition and care feasibility; abandoning follow-up removes support precisely when coordinated clinical and social assistance are needed.

options.text: Respond without blame and connect her with nutrition benefits and local food resources while revising a feasible plan
options.explanation: The barrier is access rather than knowledge; practical resource linkage and a realistic plan directly support adequate intake and ongoing pregnancy monitoring.

options.text: Repeat the same expensive food list and document intentional refusal
options.explanation: She has explained a material access limitation, so treating the problem as willful refusal misses the cause and does not create a usable nutrition plan.

options.text: Recommend fasting until delivery to keep costs down
options.explanation: Prolonged inadequate intake is already concerning, and endorsing further restriction would worsen the identified maternal nutrition problem rather than address food access.

explanation: A plan can be medically reasonable yet impossible to follow without reliable food access. This patient has identified food insecurity, so management should include a respectful response, connection to applicable nutrition programs and local resources, and adaptation of the meal plan to what is realistically available. Maternal weight and fetal growth still need follow-up, and other causes should be reassessed if the course remains abnormal. Resource eligibility varies, so the clinician should assist with screening and referral rather than guaranteeing a specific benefit or implying that disclosure automatically triggers punitive action.
objective: Treat food access as a concrete prenatal nutrition management issue.
keyPoints: Distinguish an access barrier from lack of understanding or intentional refusal.
Pair a feasible meal plan with resource linkage and clinical follow-up.

subject: Obstetrics
stem: A 28-year-old at 12 weeks of gestation asks how to avoid toxoplasmosis. She has never owned a cat and therefore believes she has no relevant exposure. She frequently tastes raw lamb while seasoning it and gardens barehanded before preparing meals. She has no symptoms and no known recent infection. Which prevention advice best addresses the risks actually described?

options.text: Cook meat to appropriate safe internal temperatures and use hand and soil hygiene with gloves for gardening
options.explanation: Undercooked meat and contaminated soil can transmit Toxoplasma even without personal cat ownership, so food preparation and gardening practices are directly relevant.

options.text: Continue tasting raw meat because only direct contact with a cat can transmit infection
options.explanation: Toxoplasma can be acquired through tissue cysts in inadequately cooked meat; limiting concern to direct cat contact overlooks a major exposure route.

options.text: Rely on washing raw meat as a complete substitute for cooking it safely
options.explanation: Surface washing does not reliably eliminate tissue cysts inside meat and can contaminate the kitchen; appropriate cooking remains an essential prevention measure.

options.text: Avoid all cooked protein foods throughout pregnancy
options.explanation: Blanket avoidance of safe cooked protein foods is unnecessary and could impair nutrition without addressing the specific preventable exposures described.

explanation: Toxoplasma acquisition is not limited to owning or touching a cat. Inadequately cooked infected meat and soil contaminated with oocysts are relevant routes. Prevention includes safe meat temperatures, avoiding raw tasting, washing produce, cleaning utensils and hands after raw meat, and gloves with handwashing for gardening. The patient is asymptomatic, so this is exposure prevention rather than proof of infection or an automatic indication for treatment. Dietary counseling should reduce specific hazards without unnecessarily eliminating safe protein sources or creating the impression that cat-free households have no risk.
objective: Address meat and soil routes when counseling about toxoplasmosis prevention during pregnancy.
keyPoints: No cat ownership does not mean no Toxoplasma exposure.
Prevent foodborne exposure without eliminating safely prepared protein foods.
